An economic reform effort was launched in 1998. Angola ranked 160 of 174 nations in the  in 2000.&lt;ref name=&quot;fastest&quot;/&gt; In April 2000 Angola started an  (IMF) Staff-Monitored Program (SMP). The program formally lapsed in June 2001, but the IMF remains engaged. In this context the Government of Angola has succeeded in unifying exchange rates and has raised fuel, electricity, and water rates. The Commercial Code, telecommunications law, and Foreign Investment Code are being modernized. A privatization effort, prepared with  assistance, has begun with the  bank. Nevertheless, a legacy of fiscal mismanagement and corruption persists. The civil war  3.8&amp;nbsp;million people, 32% of the population, by 2001.&lt;ref name=&quot;fastest&quot;/&gt; The security brought about by the 2002 peace settlement has led to the resettlement of 4 million displaced persons, thus resulting in large-scale increases in agriculture production.

Angola produced over  of diamonds in 2003,&lt;ref name=&quot;threemct&quot;&gt;&lt;/ref&gt; and production was expected to grow to  per year by 2007. In 2004, China's Eximbank approved a $2&amp;nbsp;billion line of credit to Angola to rebuild infrastructure. The economy grew 18% in 2005 and growth was expected to reach 26% in 2006 and stay above 10% for the rest of the decade.&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt; By 2020, Angola had a national debt of $76&amp;nbsp;billion, of which $20&amp;nbsp;billion is to China.&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt;

The construction industry is taking advantage of the growing economy, with various housing projects stimulated by the government such as the ''Angola Investe'' program and the '''' or '''' projects. Not all public construction projects are functional. For example, , where a whole new satellite town of Luanda, consisting of housing facilities for several hundreds of thousands of people, was completely uninhabited for over four years because of skyrocketing prices, but completely sold out after the government decreased the original price and created mortgage plans at around the election time and thus made it affordable for middle-class people. ChevronTexaco started pumping  from Block 14 in January 2000, but production decreased to  in 2007 due to poor-quality oil.&lt;ref name=&quot;opec&quot;&gt;&lt;/ref&gt; Angola joined the  on January 1, 2007.&lt;ref name=&quot;opec&quot;/&gt; Cabinda Gulf Oil Company found Malange-1, an oil reservoir in Block 14, on August 9, 2007.&lt;ref name=&quot;malfound&quot;&gt;{{cite web

Despite its abundant natural resources, output per capita is among the world's lowest. Subsistence agriculture provides the main livelihood for 85% of the population. Oil production and the supporting activities are vital to the economy, contributing about 45% to GDP and 90% of exports. Growth is almost entirely driven by rising oil production which surpassed  in late-2005 and which is expected to grow to  by 2007. Control of the oil industry is consolidated in , a conglomerate owned by the Angolan government. With revenues booming from oil exports, the government has started to implement ambitious development programs to build roads and other basic infrastructure for the nation.

In the last decade of the colonial period, Angola was a major African food exporter but now imports almost all its food. Severe wartime conditions, including extensive planting of landmines throughout the countryside, have brought agricultural activities to a near-standstill. Some efforts to recover have gone forward, however, notably in fisheries. Coffee production, though a fraction of its pre-1975 level, is sufficient for domestic needs and some exports. Expanding oil production is now almost half of GDP and 90% of exports, at . Diamonds provided much of the revenue for 's  rebellion through illicit trade. Other rich resources await development: gold, forest products, fisheries, iron ore, coffee, and fruits.&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt;

Angola produced, in 2018:

* 8.6&amp;nbsp;million tons of  (8th largest producer in the world);
* 3.5&amp;nbsp;million tons of banana (7th largest producer in the world, or the 10th largest, if we consider together with );
* 2.2&amp;nbsp;million tons of maize;
* 1.2&amp;nbsp;million tons of  (10th largest producer in the world);
* 806 thousand tons of potato;
* 597 thousand tons of  (13th largest producer in the world);
* 572 thousand tons of ;
* 355 thousand tons of ;
* 314 thousand tons of ;
* 280 thousand tons of ;
* 154 thousand tons of peanut;

In addition to smaller productions of other agricultural products, like coffee (16 thousand tons).&lt;ref&gt;[http://www.fao.org/faostat/en/#data/QC/ Angola production in 2018, by FAO]&lt;/ref&gt;




Exports in 2004 reached US$10,530,764,911. The vast majority of Angola's exports, 92% in 2004, are petroleum products. US$785&amp;nbsp;million worth of diamonds, 7.5% of exports, were sold abroad that year.&lt;ref name=&quot;exports&quot;&gt;&lt;/ref&gt; Nearly all of Angola's oil goes to the United States,  in 2006, making it the eighth largest supplier of oil to the United States, and to China,  in 2006. In the first quarter of 2008, Angola became the main exporter of oil to China.&lt;ref name=&quot;China&quot;&gt;&lt;/ref&gt; The rest of its petroleum exports go to Europe and Latin America.&lt;ref name=&quot;opec&quot;/&gt; U.S. companies account for more than half the investment in Angola, with Chevron-Texaco leading the way. The U.S. exports industrial goods and services, primarily oilfield equipment, mining equipment, chemicals, aircraft, and food, to Angola, while principally importing petroleum. Trade between Angola and South Africa exceeded US$300&amp;nbsp;million in 2007.&lt;ref name=&quot;safrica&quot;&gt;&lt;/ref&gt; From the 2000s, many Chinese have settled and started up businesses.&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt;





Angola produces and exports more petroleum than any other nation in , surpassing  first in the , then in 2022.&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt; In January 2007 Angola became a member of , before leaving in December 2023, as they wanted to expand their oil production. Under the Lourenço administration which began in 2017, the country has made efforts to incentive investments and reverse declining production, resulting in fresh investments made by international oil companies.

, , , , and  all operate in the country and represent a vast majority of daily production.&lt;ref name=&quot;oilhistory&quot;&gt;Tvedten, Inge. ''Angola: Struggle for Peace and Reconstruction'', 1997. Page 82.&lt;/ref&gt;

Block 17, operated by TotalEnergies, is Angola's biggest producing asset&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt; and is known as the Golden Block. The French major is currently executing several subsea tieback projects there, including CLOV 3 and Begonia, whose final investment decisions (FIDs) were taken in 2022.&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt;

The United Nations has criticized the Angolan government for using torture, rape, s, arbitrary detention, and disappearances, actions which Angolan government has justified on the need to maintain oil output.&lt;ref name=&quot;hroil&quot;&gt;Omeje, Kenneth C. ''High Stakes And Stakeholders: Oil Conflict And Security in Nigeria'', 2006. Page 157.&lt;/ref&gt;

Angola is the third-largest trading partner of the United States in Sub-Saharan Africa, largely because of its petroleum exports.&lt;ref name=&quot;thirdlargest&quot;&gt;United States Congress. ''Foreign Operations, Export Financing, and Related Programs Appropriations for 1998: Hearings'', 1997. Page 269.&lt;/ref&gt; The U.S. imports 7% of its oil from Angola, about three times as much as it imported from  just prior to the  in 1991. The U.S. Government has invested US$4&amp;nbsp;billion in Angola's petroleum sector.&lt;ref name=&quot;kuwait&quot;&gt;Vines, Alex. ''Angola Unravels: The Rise and Fall of the Lusaka Peace Process'', 1999. Human Rights Watch. Page 189.&lt;/ref&gt;

Oil makes up over 90% of Angola's exports.&lt;ref&gt;{{cite web

Angola is the third largest producer of diamonds in Africa and has only explored 40% of the diamond-rich territory within the country, but has had difficulty in attracting foreign investment because of corruption, human rights violations, and diamond smuggling.&lt;ref name=&quot;cfr&quot;&gt;&lt;/ref&gt; Production rose by 30% in 2006 and , the national diamond company of Angola, expects production to increase by 8% in 2007 to 10 million carats annually. The government is trying to attract foreign companies to the  of ,  and .&lt;ref name=&quot;diaexploration&quot;&gt;

Under Portuguese rule,  began mining iron in 1957, producing 1.2&amp;nbsp;million tons in 1967 and 6.2&amp;nbsp;million tons by 1971. In the early 1970s, 70% of Portuguese Angola's iron exports went to Western Europe and Japan.&lt;ref name=&quot;diaexploration&quot;/&gt; After independence in 1975, the  (1975–2002) destroyed most of the territory's mining infrastructure. The redevelopment of the Angolan mining industry started in the late 2000s.

The '''Angolan Armed Forces''' () or '''FAA''' is the military of . The FAA consist of the  (), the  () and the  (). Reported total manpower in 2021 was about 107,000.&lt;ref name=IISSp448 /&gt;  The FAA is headed by the  António Egídio de Sousa Santos since 2018, who reports to the , currently .




The FAA succeeded to the previous  (FAPLA) following the abortive  with the  (FALA), armed wing of the  (UNITA). As part of the peace agreement, troops from both armies were to be  and then integrated. Integration was never completed as UNITA and FALA went back to war in 1992. Later, consequences for FALA personnel in Luanda were harsh with FAPLA veterans persecuting their erstwhile opponents in certain areas and reports of .


The Angolan Armed Forces were created on 9 October 1991. The institutionalization of the FAA was made in the , signed in 1991, between the Angolan Government and UNITA. The principles that would govern the FAA were defined in a joint proposal presented on September 24, 1991, and approved on 9 October. On 14 November 1991, Generals João Baptista de Matos and Abílio Kamalata Numa were appointed to the Superior Command of the Armed Forces. The ceremony took place at the , and was presided over by the then-minister França Vandúnem.&lt;ref&gt; FORÇAS ARMADAS ANGOLANAS|url=https://faa.ao/pagina/historia-cultura|access-date=2021-06-29|website=faa.ao|archive-date=May 25, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210525173050/https://faa.ao/pagina/historia-cultura|url-status=dead}}&lt;/ref&gt;






The Army (''Exército'') is the land component of the FAA. It is organized in six military regions (Cabinda, Luanda, North, Center, East and South), with an infantry division being based in each one. Distributed by the six military regions / infantry divisions, there are 25 motorized infantry brigades, one tank brigade and one engineering brigade. The Army also includes an artillery regiment, the Military Artillery School, the Army Military Academy, an anti-aircraft defense group, a composite land artillery group, a military police regiment, a logistical transportation regiment and a field artillery brigade. The Army further includes the Special Forces Brigade (including Commandos and Special Operations units), but this unit is under the direct command of the General Staff of the FAA.




The  (FANA, ''Força Aérea Nacional de Angola'') is the air component of the FAA. It is organized in six aviation regiments, each including several squadrons. To each of the regiments correspond an air base. Besides the aviation regiments, there is also a Pilot Training School.

The Air Force's personnel total about 8,000; its equipment includes transport aircraft and six Russian-manufactured  .&lt;ref&gt;IISS Military Balance 2013, 494&lt;/ref&gt; In 2002, one was lost during the civil war with UNITA forces.&lt;ref&gt;[http://www.globaldefence.net/streitkraefte-der-welt/afrika/346-angola.html globaldefence.net: Angolan Armed Forces]  retrieved August 22, 2011 (de)&lt;/ref&gt;

In 1991, the Air Force/Air Defense Forces had 8,000 personnel and 90 combat-capable aircraft, including 22 fighters, 59 fighter ground attack aircraft and 16 attack helicopters.




The Angola Navy (MGA, ''Marinha de Guerra de Angola'') is the naval component of the FAA. It is organized in two naval zones (North and South), with naval bases in Luanda, Lobito and Moçâmedes. It includes a Marines Brigade and a Marines School, based in Ambriz. The Navy numbers about 1,000 personnel and operates only a handful of small patrol craft and barges.

The Navy has been neglected and ignored as a military arm mainly due to the guerrilla struggle against the Portuguese and the nature of the civil war. From the early 1990s to the present the Angolan Navy has shrunk from around 4,200 personnel to around 1,000, resulting in the loss of skills and expertise needed to maintain equipment. Portugal has been providing training through its Technical Military Cooperation (CTM) programme. The Navy is requesting procurement of a frigate, three corvettes, three offshore patrol vessel and additional fast patrol boats.

Most of the vessels in the navy's inventory dates back from the 1980s or earlier, and many of its ships are inoperable due to age and lack of maintenance. However the navy acquired new boats from Spain and France in the 1990s. Germany has delivered several  for border protection in 2011.

In September 2014 it was reported that the Angolan Navy would acquire seven s from Brazil as part of a Technical Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) covering the production of the vessels as part of Angola's Naval Power Development Programme (Pronaval).&lt;ref name=DWMacae&gt;&lt;/ref&gt; The military of Angola aims to modernize its naval capability, presumably due to a rise in maritime piracy within the Gulf of Guinea which may have an adverse effect on the country's economy.

The navy's current known inventory includes the following:

* 
** 4 Mandume class craft (Bazan Cormoran type, refurbished in 2009)
* s
** 3 18.3m long Patrulheiro patrol boats (refurbished in 2002)&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt;
** 5 ARESA PVC-170
** 2 s
* Fisheries Patrol Boats
** Ngola Kiluange and Nzinga Mbandi (delivered in September and October 2012 from )(Operated by Navy personnel under the Ministry of Agriculture, Rural Development and Fisheries)
** 28-metre FRV 2810 (Pensador) (Operated by Navy personnel under the Ministry of Agriculture, Rural Development and Fisheries)&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt;
* Landing craft

The FAA include several types of special forces, namely the Commandos, the Special Operations and the Marines. The Angolan special forces follow the general model of the analogous Portuguese special forces, receiving similar training.

The Commandos and the Special forces are part of the Special Forces Brigade (BRIFE, ''Brigada de Forças Especiais''), based at Cabo Ledo, in the . The BRIFE includes two battalions of commandos, a battalion of special operations and sub-units of combat support and service support. The BRIFE also included the Special Actions Group (GAE, ''Grupo de Ações Especiais''), which is presently inactive and that was dedicated to long range reconnaissance, covert and sabotage operations. In the Cabo Ledo base is also installed the Special Forces Training School (EFFE, ''Escola de Formação de Forças Especiais''). Both the BRIFE and the EFFE are directly under the Directorate of Special Forces of the General Staff of the Armed Forces.

The marines (''fuzileiros navais'') constitute the Marines Brigade of the Angolan Navy. The Marines Brigade is not permanently dependent of the Directorate of Special Forces, but can detach their units and elements to be put under the command of that body for the conduction of exercises or real operations. The Marines have a special forces unit known as Special Operations Marines(FOE, Fuzileiros Operaçües Especiais).&lt;ref&gt;Bond, Jason (October 7, 2015), &quot;US, UK Royal Marines work with West African partners during Africa Partnership Station [Image 4 of 20]&quot; Defense Visual Information Distribution Information Service, US Department of Defense, https://www.dvidshub.net/image/2293338/us-uk-royal-marines-work-with-west-african-partners-during-africa-partnership-station, Date accessed: February 2, 2025&lt;/ref&gt;

Since the disbandment of the Angolan Parachute Battalion in 2004, the FAA do not have a specialized paratrooper unit. However, elements of the commandos, special operations and marines are parachute qualified.


The Directorate of People's Defense and Territorial Troops of the Defence Ministry or ODP was established in late 1975. It had 600,000 members, having personnel in virtually every village by 1979. It had both armed and unarmed units dispersed in villages throughout the country.&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt; The People's Vigilance Brigades () also serve a similar purpose.&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt;




The Military Academy () is a military university public higher education establishment whose mission is to train officers of the Permanent Staff of the Army. It has been in operation since 21 August 2009 by presidential decree.&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt; Its headquarters are in . It trains in the following specialties:&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt;


*Infantry
*Tanks
*Land Artillery
*Anti-Air Defense
*Military Engineering
*Logistics
*Telecommunications
*Hidden Direction of Troops
*Military Administration
*Armament and Technique
*Chemical Defense
*Operational Military Intelligence
*Technical Repair and Maintenance Platoon of Auto and Armored Technique

* Pilot Basic Training School ()







The  of the FAA is the Main Military Hospital. It has the following lineage:

* 1961 – Evacuation Infirmary
* 1962 – Military Hospital of Luanda
* 1975 – Military Hospital
* 1976 – Central Military Hospital
* 1989 – Main Military Hospital

It provides specialized medical assistance in accordance with the military health system; It also promotes post-graduate education and scientific research. Currently, the Main Military Hospital serves 39 special medical specialties. It is a headed by a Director General whose main supporting body is the board of directors.&lt;ref&gt; FORÇAS ARMADAS ANGOLANAS|url=https://faa.ao/pagina/hospital-militar-principal|access-date=2021-06-28|website=faa.ao|archive-date=May 25, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210525173503/https://faa.ao/pagina/hospital-militar-principal|url-status=dead}}&lt;/ref&gt;


The Supreme Military Court is the highest organ of the hierarchy of s. The Presiding Judge, the Deputy Presiding Judge and the other Counselor Judges of the Supreme Military Court are appointed by the President of the Republic. The composition, organization, powers and functioning of the Supreme Military Court are established by law.&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt;


The FAA maintains Portuguese-style military bands in all three branches and in individual units. The primary band is the 100-member Music Band of the Presidential Security Household.&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt; The music band of the Army Command was created on 16 June 1994&lt;ref&gt;http://m.portalangop.co.ao/angola/pt_pt/mobile/noticias/politica/2017/1/8/Moxico-FAA-preve-criar-bandas-musica-nas-unidades-militares,dd07f366-3490-46c4-8298-7947ecc750c7.html?version=mobile &lt;/ref&gt; and four years later, on 15 August 1998, the National Air Force created a music band within an artistic brigade.&lt;ref&gt;http://tpa.sapo.ao/noticias/cultura/banda-da-forca-aerea-realiza-hoje-espectaculo-no-maan &lt;/ref&gt; The navy has its own marching band, as well as a small musical group known as ''Banda 10 de Julho'' (10 July Band), based at the  Naval Base.&lt;ref&gt;http://jornaldeangola.sapo.ao/cultura/musica/banda_da_marinha_de_guerra_grava_a_voz_do_marinheiro &lt;/ref&gt;


The FAPLA's main counterinsurgency effort was directed against UNITA in the southeast, and its conventional capabilities were demonstrated principally in the undeclared .&lt;ref name=&quot;ReferenceA&quot;&gt;&lt;/ref&gt; The FAPLA first performed its external assistance mission with the dispatch of 1,000 to 1,500 troops to  in 1977 to bolster the socialist regime of President Manuel Pinto da Costa. During the next several years, Angolan forces conducted joint exercises with their counterparts and exchanged technical operational visits. The Angolan expeditionary force was reduced to about 500 in early 1985.

The Angolan Armed Forces were controversially involved in training the armed forces of fellow  states  and Guinea-Bissau. In the case of the latter, the  was cited by the coup leaders as due to Angola's involvement in trying to &quot;reform&quot; the military in connivance with the civilian leadership.

Occasionally skirmishes on the -Angola border happening, sometimes also in connection with the . In 2020 one Angolan soldier died after a gun battle with congolese forces in  on DRC territory.&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt; A presence during the unrest in , 2010–2011, were not officially confirmed. However, the , citing '''', said that among President 's guards were 92 personnel of President Dos Santos's .&lt;ref&gt;[https://www.faz.net/aktuell/politik/ausland/elfenbeinkueste-gbagbos-letzte-trumpfkarte-als-maertyrer-sterben-1628414.html Gbagbos letzte Trumpfkarte: als Märtyrer sterben] , April 7, 2011&lt;/ref&gt; Angola is basically interested in the participation of the FAA operations of the  and has formed special units for this purpose.

In 2021, the Angolan Parliament approved integration of FAA into  (SADC)'s mission for peace in , Mozambique. Angola sent a team of 20 officers to participate.&lt;ref&gt; English.news.cn |url=http://www.xinhuanet.com/english/africa/2021-07/28/c_1310092087.htm |access-date=2022-05-10 |website=www.xinhuanet.com |archive-date=October 25, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211025093503/http://www.xinhuanet.com/english/africa/2021-07/28/c_1310092087.htm |url-status=dead }}&lt;/ref&gt;

The '''foreign relations of Angola''' are based on Angola's strong support of  as the  is dependent on U.S. foreign aid.
From 1975 to 1989, Angola was aligned with the , in particular the ,&lt;ref name=&quot;U.S. Department of State 2008&quot;&gt;}}&lt;/ref&gt; , and .&lt;ref name=&quot;U.S. Department of State 2008&quot; /&gt; Since then, it has focused on improving relationships with , cultivating links with other Portuguese-speaking countries, and asserting its own national interests in Central Africa through military and diplomatic intervention.&lt;ref name=&quot;U.S. Department of State 2008&quot; /&gt; In 1993, it established formal diplomatic relations with the United States.&lt;ref name=&quot;U.S. Department of State 2008&quot; /&gt; It has entered the  as a vehicle for improving ties with its largely Anglophone neighbors to the south.&lt;ref name=&quot;U.S. Department of State 2008&quot; /&gt;  and  joined Angola in its military intervention in the , where Angolan troops remain in support of the  government.&lt;ref name=&quot;U.S. Department of State 2008&quot; /&gt; It also has intervened in the  (Brazzaville) in support of Denis Sassou-Nguesso in the civil war.&lt;ref name=&quot;U.S. Department of State 2008&quot; /&gt;

Since 1998, Angola has successfully worked with the  to impose and carry out sanctions on .&lt;ref name=&quot;U.S. Department of State 2001&quot;&gt;}}&lt;/ref&gt; More recently, it has extended those efforts to controls on , the primary source of revenue for UNITA during the Civil War that ended in 2002.&lt;ref name=&quot;U.S. Department of State 2001&quot; /&gt; At the same time, Angola has promoted the revival of the Community of Portuguese-Speaking Countries () as a forum for cultural exchange and expanding ties with  (its former ruler) and Brazil (which shares many cultural affinities with Angola) in particular.&lt;ref name=&quot;U.S. Department of State 2008&quot; /&gt;&lt;ref name=&quot;U.S. Department of State 2001&quot;/&gt; Angola is a member of the  (PMAESA).

 '''Albert Sidney Johnston''' (February 2, 1803 – April 6, 1862) was an American military officer who served as a  in three different armies: the , the , and the . He saw extensive combat during his 34-year military career, fighting actions in the , the , the , the , and the , where he died on the battlefield.

Considered by Confederate States President  to be the finest general officer in the Confederacy before the later emergence of , he was killed early in the Civil War at the  on April 6, 1862. Johnston was the highest-ranking officer on either side killed during the war. Davis believed the loss of General Johnston &quot;was the turning point of our fate.&quot;

Johnston was unrelated to Confederate general .


Johnston was born in , the youngest son of Dr. John and Abigail (Harris) Johnston. His father was a native of .  He was a grandson of Revolutionary War patriot Edward Harris. Although Albert Johnston was born in Kentucky, he lived much of his life in , which he considered his home.&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt; He was first educated at  in , where he met fellow student . Both were appointed to the  at , Davis two years behind Johnston.&lt;ref name=&quot;Woodworth46&quot;&gt;Woodworth, p. 46.&lt;/ref&gt; In 1826,&lt;ref name=EB1911&gt;Chisholm, p. 472&lt;/ref&gt; Johnston graduated eighth of 41 cadets in his class from West Point with a commission as a   in the .&lt;ref name=&quot;Eicher322&quot;&gt;Eicher, p. 322.&lt;/ref&gt;

Johnston was assigned to New York and  posts. In August 1827, he participated in the expedition to capture , the rebellious Winnebago chief. Johnston later wrote: &quot;I must confess that I consider Red Bird one of the noblest and most dignified men I ever saw... He said: 'I have offended. I sacrifice myself to save my country.'&quot;&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt; Johnston served in the brief  of 1832 as chief of staff to Brevet Brigadier General . The commander praised Johnston for &quot;talents of the first order, a gallant soldier by profession and education and a gentleman of high standing and integrity.&quot;&lt;ref name=&quot;Roland&quot; /&gt;

In April 1834, Johnston resigned from the United States Army to care for his wife, who had contracted . They moved back to Kentucky, but she died in August 1835. Johnston was then approached by an agent from the , who requested his aid in the defense of the country from invasion by the . Johnston agreed, and leaving his two children in the care of relatives in Kentucky, traveled south.&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt;


Johnston moved to Texas in 1836 and&lt;ref name=EB1911/&gt; enlisted as a  in the Texian Army&lt;ref name=EB1911/&gt; after the  from the Republic of Mexico. He was named  as a  in the Republic of Texas Army on August 5, 1836. On January 31, 1837, he became senior  in command of the Texas Army.

On February 5, 1837, Johnston fought in a duel with Texas Brigadier General , who was angered and offended by Johnston's promotion. Huston had been the acting commander of the army and perceived Johnston's appointment as a slight from the Texas government. Johnston was shot through the hip and severely wounded, requiring him to relinquish his post during his recovery.&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt;

Afterward, Johnston said he fought Huston &quot;as a public duty... he had little respect for the practice of dueling.&quot; He believed that the &quot;safety of the republic depended upon the efficiency of the army... and upon the good discipline and subordination of the troops, which could only be secured by their obedience to their legal commander. General Huston embodied the lawless spirit in the army, which had to be met and controlled at whatever personal peril.&quot;&lt;ref&gt;Johnston, pp. 80&lt;/ref&gt;

Many years later, Huston said that the duel was &quot;a shameful piece of business, and I wouldn't do it again under any circumstances... Why, when I reflect upon the circumstances, I hate myself... that one act blackened all the good ones of my life. But I couldn't challenge Congress; and President , although a duelist, was too far above me in rank. Well, thank God I didn't kill him.&quot;&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt;

On December 22, 1838, , the second president of the , appointed Johnston as Secretary of War. He defended the Texas border against Mexican invasion. In 1839, he campaigned against Native Americans in northern Texas during the Cherokee War of 1838–39. At the , Johnston and Vice President  were both cited in the commander's report &quot;for active exertions on the field&quot; and &quot;having behaved in such a manner as reflects great credit upon themselves.&quot;&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt;

In February 1840, Johnston resigned his position as Secretary of War and returned to Kentucky, marrying for the second time. He purchased a large  in , Texas, named &quot;China Grove.&quot; He leased the property out and moved his family to Galveston.


 at , Utah Territory, winter of 1858–59]]
When the United States declared war on Mexico in May 1846, Johnston rode 400 miles from his home in  to  to volunteer for service in Brigadier General 's Army of Occupation. Johnston was elected as  of the 1st Texas Rifle Volunteers but the enlistments of his soldiers ran out just before the army's advance on , so Taylor appointed him as the inspector general of Brigadier General  division of volunteers. Johnston convinced a few volunteers of his former regiment to stay on and fight.

During the , Butler was wounded and carried to the rear, and Johnston assumed an active leadership role in the division. Future U.S. general, , was with Johnston at Monterrey and wrote: &quot;It was through [Johnston's] agency, mainly, that our division was saved from a cruel slaughter... The coolness and magnificent presence [that he] displayed on this field... left an impression on my mind that I have never forgotten.&quot;&lt;ref name=&quot;Roland&quot;&gt;Roland, pp. 243&lt;/ref&gt; General Taylor considered Johnston &quot;the best soldier he had ever commanded.&quot;&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt;

Johnston resigned from the army just after the battle of Monterrey in October 1846. He had promised his wife, Eliza, that he would only volunteer for six months' service. In addition, President 's administration's preference for officers associated with the Democratic Party prevented the promotion of those, such as Johnston, who were perceived as Whigs:



He remained on his plantation after the war until he was appointed by later 12th president  to the  as a  and was made a paymaster in December 1849 for a district of Texas encompassing the military posts from the upper Colorado River to the upper Trinity River.&lt;ref name=EB1911/&gt; He served in that role for more than five years, making six tours and traveling more than  annually on the Indian frontier of Texas. He served on the Texas frontier at  and elsewhere in the western United States.

In 1855, 14th president  appointed him colonel of the new 2nd U.S. Cavalry (the unit that preceded the modern ), a new regiment, which he organized, his lieutenant colonel being Robert E. Lee, and his majors  and .&lt;ref name=EB1911/&gt; Other subordinates in this unit included , , , , , R.W. Johnson, , and , all future Civil War generals.&lt;ref&gt;Johnston, pp. 185&lt;/ref&gt; On March 31, 1856, Johnston received a promotion to temporary command of the entire Department of Texas. He campaigned aggressively against the , writing to his daughter that &quot;the Indians harass our frontiers and the 2nd Cavalry and other troops thrash them wherever they catch them.&quot;&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt; In March 1857, Brigadier General  was appointed permanent commander of the department and Johnston returned to his position as colonel of the 2nd Cavalry.


As a key figure in the , Johnston took command of the U.S. forces dispatched to crush the supposed  rebellion in November 1857. Their objective was to install  as governor of the Utah Territory, replacing , and restore U.S. legal authority in the region. As Johnston had replaced Brigadier General  in command, he only joined the army after it had already departed for Utah. Johnston's adjutant general, and future U.S. general in the Civil War, Major  wrote: &quot;Experienced on the Plains and of established reputation for energy, courage, and resources, [Johnston's] presence restored confidence at all points, and encouraged the weak-hearted and panic-stricken multitude. The long chain of wagons, kinked, tangled, and hard to move, uncoiled and went forward smoothly.&quot;&lt;ref&gt;Johnston, pp. 211&lt;/ref&gt;

Johnston worked tirelessly over the next few months to maintain the effectiveness of his army in the harsh winter environment at Fort Bridger, Wyoming. Major Porter wrote to an associate: &quot;Col. Johnston has done everything to add to the efficiency of the command – and put it in a condition to sustain the dignity and honor of the country – More he cannot do… Don't let any one come here over Col. Johnston – It would be much against the wishes and hopes of everyone here – who would gladly see him a Brigadier General.&quot;&lt;ref&gt;Roland, pp. 202&lt;/ref&gt; Even the Mormons commended Johnston's actions, with the Salt Lake City ''Deseret News'' reporting that &quot;It takes a cool brain and good judgment to maintain a contented army and healthy camp through a stormy winter in the Wasatch Mountains.&quot;&lt;ref&gt;Deseret News (1858). Edition published October 13, 1858, Salt Lake City, Utah Territory.&lt;/ref&gt;

Johnston and his troops hoped for war. They had learned of the  and wanted revenge against the Mormons. However, a peaceful resolution was reached after the army had endured the harsh winter at Fort Bridger. In late June 1858, Johnston led the army through Salt Lake City without incident to establish  some 50 miles distant. In a report to the War Department, Johnston reported that &quot;horrible crimes… have been perpetrated in this territory, crimes of a magnitude and of an apparently studied refinement in atrocity, hardly to be conceived of, and which have gone unwhipped of justice.&quot;&lt;ref&gt;Johnston, pp. 239&lt;/ref&gt; Nevertheless, Johnston's army peacefully occupied the Utah Territory. U.S. Army Commander-in-Chief, Major General , was delighted with Johnston's performance during the campaign and recommended his promotion to brevet : &quot;Colonel Johns[t]on is more than a good officer – he is a God send to the country thro' the army.&quot;&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt; The Senate confirmed Johnston's promotion on March 24, 1858.

Although disappointed to have never been given the opportunity to put the Mormons to the sword, Johnston’s time in the Utah Territory was profitable. His soldiers provided protection to emigrant wagon trains heading to California and Oregon and his officers discovered more efficient routes traversing the region. In the summer of 1859, Johnston provided carers, wagons, and an armed escort for eighteen children discovered to have survived the Mountain Meadows Massacre for their journey back to the east.


While serving in the Utah Territory, Major Porter reported that &quot;Colonel Johnston took every occasion to bring the Indians within knowledge and influence of the army, and induced numerous chiefs to come to his camp... Colonel Johnston was ever kind, but firm, and dignified to them... The Utes, Pi-Utes, Bannocks, and other tribes, visited Colonel Johnston, and all went away expressing themselves pleased, assuring him that so long as he remained they would prove his friends, which the colonel told them would be best for them. Thus he effectively destroyed all influence of the Mormons over them, and insured friendly treatment to travelers to and from California and Oregon.&quot;&lt;ref&gt;Johnston, p. 235&lt;/ref&gt;

In August 1859, parts of Johnston's Army of Utah were implicated as participants in an alleged massacre at , a retaliation against an Indian massacre of an emigrant train to California. There are conflicting reports of the event and Johnston only referenced it in a November 1859 report to Gen. Scott. He wrote: &quot;I have ascertained that three [emigrant] parties were robbed, and ten or twelve of their members, comprising men, women, and children, murdered... The perpetrators of the robbery of the first party were severely chastised by a detachment of dragoons, under the command of Lieutenant Gay. The troops failed to discover the robbers of the last two parties that were attacked. They are supposed to be vagabonds from the Shoshonee (sic) or Snake and Bannack (sic) Indians, whose chiefs deny any complicity with these predatory bands. There is abundant evidence to prove that these robber bands are accompanied by white men, and probably instigated and led by them. On that account I am inclined to believe the disclaimer of the Indians referred to, of having any knowledge of the robberies or any share in the plunder.&quot; The only conflicting report of the incident to that of Gen. Johnston and Lieut. Gay was the account of  (written in 1910, about 51 years later) and oral histories.&lt;ref&gt;Senate of the United States; First Session of the 36th Congress, 1859–60; No. 42, p. 26&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref&gt;Wilson, pp. 165&lt;/ref&gt;

In late February 1860, Johnston received orders from the War Department recalling him to Washington D.C. to prepare for a new assignment. &quot;In Southern Utah, an Indian chief, to prove his friendship and warn off prowling clansmen, ran on foot for several days beside his wagon, keeping pace with the trot of the mules. General Johnston on parting gave him among other presents, to his extravagant delight, a 'coat of many colors'... a patchwork quilt that had served through the campaign.&quot;&lt;ref&gt;Johnston, pp. 246&lt;/ref&gt;  Johnston spent 1860 in Kentucky until December 21, when he sailed for  to take command of the .&lt;ref name=&quot;EB1911&quot; /&gt; In the spring of 1861, Johnston dispatched small parties of troops to patrol northern California in response to reports of Native American raids on settlers in the region. He warned his officers that there must be &quot;no indiscriminate slaughter of the guilty with the innocent&quot; and there were no further incidents.&lt;ref name=&quot;Roland&quot;/&gt;


Johnston's eldest son recalled that &quot;General Johnston's views in regard to slavery were those generally held in the South, where he was born and brought up, and with whose social structure he had been identified... they were the beliefs of eight millions of people...&quot;&lt;ref&gt;Johnston, pp. 258&lt;/ref&gt; In 1846, he owned four slaves in Texas.&lt;ref&gt;Roland, p. 141.&lt;/ref&gt; In 1855, having discovered that a slave was stealing from the Army payroll, Johnston refused to have him physically punished and instead sold him for $1,000 to recoup the losses. Johnston explained that &quot;whipping will not restore what is lost and it will not benefit the [culprit], whom a lifetime of kind treatment has failed to make honest.&quot;&lt;ref&gt;Roland, p. 166.&lt;/ref&gt; In 1856, he called  &quot;fanatical, idolatrous, negro worshipping&quot; in a letter to his son, fearing that the abolitionists would incite a slave revolt in the Southern states.&lt;ref&gt;Roland, p. 182.&lt;/ref&gt; Upon moving to California, Johnston sold one slave to his son and freed another, Randolph Hughes, or &quot;Ran&quot;, who agreed to accompany the family on the condition of a $12/month contract for five more years of servitude. Ran accompanied Johnston throughout the American Civil War until the latter's death.&lt;ref&gt;Roland, p. 242.&lt;/ref&gt;



In the lead up to the , rumors began to circulate that Johnston, as a known sympathizer of the southern states, would turn over control of the Federal military installations in  to clandestine southern paramilitary organizations. So alarmed was the Governor of California, , that he visited Johnston to discuss the allegations. Johnston responded: “I have spent the greater part of my life in the service of my country, and while I hold her commission [I] shall serve her honorably and faithfully. I shall protect her public property, and not a cartridge or a percussion cap belonging to her shall pass to any enemy while I am here as her representative. There is no man in the Union more sorely afflicted than I am at the occurrences now taking place. I have been long identified with Texas, her interests and public men, and her action may control my future destiny. But in any event I shall give due notice and turn over intact my department to my successor.&quot;&lt;ref&gt;Roland, pp. 245-246&lt;/ref&gt; Johnston strengthened the garrisons of all the military assets in San Francisco, transferred 10,000 muskets and their ammunition from the Bernicia arsenal to the more secure fortress on  Island, and ordered heightened surveillance of all boats and passengers operating in San Francisco Harbor.

Like many regular army officers from the Southern United States, Johnston opposed secession. Nevertheless, he resigned his commission soon after he heard of the Confederate states' declarations of secession. The War Department accepted it on May 6, 1861, effective May 3.&lt;ref&gt;Johnston, p. 273.&lt;/ref&gt; On April 28, he moved to Los Angeles, the home of his wife's brother . Considering staying in California with his wife and children, Johnston remained there until May, but news of the secession of Texas, the shelling of Fort Sumter, and the mobilization of 75,000 Union volunteers to suppress the rebellion compelled Johnston to act. “It seems like fate that Texas has made me a Rebel twice,” he commented to his wife. Johnston enlisted in the  (a pro-Southern militia unit) as a private, leaving  on May 27.&lt;ref&gt;Johnston, pp. 185.&lt;/ref&gt; He participated in their trek across the Southwestern deserts to Texas, crossing the  into the  on July 4, 1861. His escort was commanded by , Undersheriff of Los Angeles, who remained at Johnston's side until he was killed.&lt;ref&gt; ''Los Angeles Star,'' Vol. XIII, No. 32, December 12, 1863.&lt;/ref&gt;

Early in the Civil War, Confederate President  decided that the Confederacy would attempt to hold as much territory as possible, distributing military forces around its borders and coasts.&lt;ref&gt;Woodworth, pp. 18–19.&lt;/ref&gt; In the summer of 1861, Davis appointed several generals to defend Confederate lines from the Mississippi River east to the Allegheny Mountains.&lt;ref&gt;Woodworth, pp. 17–33.&lt;/ref&gt; Aged 58 when the war began, Johnston was old by Army standards. He came east to offer his service for the Confederacy without having been promised anything, merely hoping for an assignment.

The most sensitive, and in many ways, the most crucial areas, along the Mississippi River and in western Tennessee along the  and the  rivers&lt;ref&gt;Woodworth, pp. 20–22&lt;/ref&gt; were placed under the command of   and  . The latter had initially been in command in Tennessee as that State's top general.&lt;ref&gt;Woodworth, pp. 30–32.&lt;/ref&gt; Their impolitic occupation of , on September 3, 1861, two days before Johnston arrived in the Confederacy's capital of , after his cross-country journey, drove Kentucky from its stated neutrality.&lt;ref&gt;Woodworth, pp. 35, 45.&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref&gt;Long, p. 114.&lt;/ref&gt; The majority of Kentuckians allied with the U.S. camp.&lt;ref&gt;Woodworth, pp. 39, 50.&lt;/ref&gt; Polk and Pillow's action gave U.S.   an excuse to take control of the strategically located town of , without raising the ire of most Kentuckians and the pro-U.S. majority in the State legislature.&lt;ref&gt;Woodworth, p. 39.&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref&gt;Long, p. 115.&lt;/ref&gt;


On September 10, 1861, Johnston was assigned to command the huge area of the Confederacy west of the Allegheny Mountains, except for coastal areas. He became commander of the Confederacy's western armies in the area often called the  or Western Military Department.&lt;ref name=&quot;Woodworth51&quot;&gt;Woodworth, p. 51.&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref name=&quot;Long, p. 116&quot;&gt;Long, p. 116.&lt;/ref&gt; Johnston's appointment as a  by his friend and admirer Jefferson Davis had already been confirmed by the Confederate Senate on August 31, 1861. The appointment had been backdated to rank from May 30, 1861, making him the second-highest-ranking general in the Confederate States Army. Only Adjutant General and Inspector General  ranked ahead of him.&lt;ref&gt;Eicher, ''Civil War High Commands.'' p.&amp;nbsp;807. From General Command Line List. Weigley, p.&amp;nbsp;110. McPherson, p.&amp;nbsp;394.&lt;/ref&gt; After his appointment, Johnston immediately headed for his new territory.&lt;ref name=&quot;Woodworth52&quot;&gt;Woodworth, p. 52.&lt;/ref&gt; He was permitted to call on Arkansas, Tennessee, and Mississippi governors for new troops. However, politics largely stifled this authority, especially concerning Mississippi.&lt;ref name=&quot;Woodworth51&quot;/&gt; On September 13, 1861, Johnston ordered Brig. Gen.  with 4,000 men to occupy  in Kentucky to block U.S. troops from coming into eastern Tennessee. The Kentucky legislature had voted to side with the United States after the occupation of Columbus by Polk.&lt;ref name=&quot;Woodworth52&quot;/&gt; By September 18, Johnston had Brig. Gen.  with another 4,000 men blocking the railroad route to Tennessee at .&lt;ref name=&quot;Woodworth52&quot;/&gt;&lt;ref&gt;Long, p. 119.&lt;/ref&gt;

Johnston had fewer than 40,000 men spread throughout Kentucky, Tennessee, Arkansas, and Missouri.&lt;ref name=&quot;Woodworth53&quot;&gt;Woodworth, p. 53.&lt;/ref&gt; Of these, 10,000 were in Missouri under  Maj. Gen. .&lt;ref name=&quot;Woodworth53&quot;/&gt; Johnston did not quickly gain many recruits when he first requested them from the governors, but his more serious problem was lacking sufficient arms and ammunition for the troops he already had.&lt;ref name=&quot;Woodworth53&quot;/&gt; As the Confederate government concentrated efforts on the units in the East, they gave Johnston small numbers of reinforcements and minimal amounts of arms and material.&lt;ref name=&quot;Woodworth55&quot;&gt;Woodworth, p. 55.&lt;/ref&gt; Johnston maintained his defense by conducting raids and other measures to make it appear he had larger forces than he did, a strategy that worked for several months.&lt;ref name=&quot;Woodworth55&quot;/&gt; Johnston's tactics had so annoyed and confused U.S. Brig. Gen.  in Kentucky that he became paranoid and mentally unstable. In a letter to his wife, Sherman stated: &quot;I find myself riding a whirlwind unable to guide the storm. Rumors and reports pour in on me of the overwhelming force collected in front across Green River... To advance would be madness and to stand still folly... the idea of going down to history with a fame such as threatens me nearly makes me crazy, indeed I may be so now.&quot;&lt;ref&gt;Goggin, pp. 64&lt;/ref&gt;  Sherman overestimated Johnston's forces and was relieved by Brig. Gen.  on November 9, 1861. However, in his ''Memoirs'', Sherman strongly rebutted this account.&lt;ref&gt;Woodworth, pp. 55–56&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref&gt;Long, p. 138.&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref&gt;McPherson, p. 394 says Johnston had 70,000 troops to defend his territory between the Appalachians and the Ozarks by the end of 1861.&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref&gt;''The Memoirs of General W. T. Sherman'' (1885), Chapter IX https://www.gutenberg.org/files/4361/4361-h/4361-h.htm&lt;/ref&gt;


 (a heavily  during the Civil War) was occupied for the Confederacy by two unimpressive brigadier generals appointed by Jefferson Davis: , a brave but untrained and inexperienced officer, and soon-to-be Maj. Gen. , a former U.S. Army officer with apparent alcohol problems.&lt;ref&gt;Woodworth, p. 61&lt;/ref&gt; While Crittenden was away in Richmond, Zollicoffer moved his forces to the north bank of the upper Cumberland River near Mill Springs (now ), putting the river to his back and his forces into a trap.&lt;ref&gt;Woodworth, p. 65.&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref&gt;Long, pp. 161–162.&lt;/ref&gt; Zollicoffer decided it was impossible to obey orders to return to the other side of the river because of the scarcity of transport and proximity of U.S. troops.&lt;ref name=&quot;Woodworth, p. 66&quot;&gt;Woodworth, p. 66.&lt;/ref&gt; When U.S. Brig. Gen.  moved against the Confederates, Crittenden decided to attack one of the two parts of Thomas's command at Logan's Cross Roads near Mill Springs before the U.S. forces could unite.&lt;ref name=&quot;Woodworth, p. 66&quot;/&gt; At the  on January 19, 1862, the ill-prepared Confederates, after a night march in the rain, attacked the U.S. soldiers with some initial success.&lt;ref&gt;Woodworth, pp. 66–67.&lt;/ref&gt; As the battle progressed, Zollicoffer was killed and the Confederates were turned back and routed by a U.S. bayonet charge, their force of 4,000 suffering 533 casualties, while Crittenden's conduct in the battle was so inept that subordinates accused him of being drunk.&lt;ref&gt;Woodworth, p. 67.&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref&gt;Long, p. 162.&lt;/ref&gt; The Confederate troops who escaped were assigned to other units as General Crittenden faced an investigation of his conduct.&lt;ref&gt;Woodworth, p. 69.&lt;/ref&gt;

After the Confederate defeat at Mill Springs, Davis sent Johnston a brigade and a few other scattered reinforcements. He also assigned him Gen. , who was supposed to attract recruits because of his victories early in the war and act as a competent subordinate for Johnston.&lt;ref&gt;Woodworth, pp. 71–72.&lt;/ref&gt; The brigade was led by Brig. Gen. , a former Governor of Virginia. After Johnston, Beauregard, and Hardee, Floyd was the most senior officer in the Western Department by virtue of his early date of commission as a general. Floyd took command at  as the senior general present just before U.S. Brig. Gen.  attacked the fort.&lt;ref&gt;Woodworth, pp. 80, 84.&lt;/ref&gt; Historians believe the assignment of Beauregard to the west stimulated U.S. commanders to attack the forts before Beauregard could make a difference in the theater. U.S. Army officers heard that he was bringing 15 regiments with him, but this was an exaggeration of his forces.&lt;ref name=&quot;Woodworth7278&quot;&gt;Woodworth, pp. 72, 78.&lt;/ref&gt;


Based on the assumption that Kentucky neutrality would act as a shield against a direct invasion from the north, circumstances that no longer applied in September 1861, Tennessee initially had sent men to Virginia and concentrated defenses in the Mississippi Valley.&lt;ref&gt;Woodworth, p. 54.&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref&gt;Eicher, ''The Longest Night''. pp. 111–113.&lt;/ref&gt; Even before Johnston arrived in Tennessee, construction of two forts had been started to defend the  and the  rivers, which provided avenues into the State from the north.&lt;ref name=&quot;Woodworth56&quot;&gt;Woodworth, p. 56.&lt;/ref&gt; Both forts were located in Tennessee to respect Kentucky neutrality, but these were not in ideal locations.&lt;ref name=&quot;Woodworth56&quot;/&gt;&lt;ref name=&quot;Long142&quot;&gt;Long, p. 142&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref&gt;Weigley, p. 108&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref&gt;McPherson, p. 393.&lt;/ref&gt;  on the Tennessee River was in an unfavorable low-lying location, commanded by hills on the Kentucky side of the river.&lt;ref name=&quot;Woodworth56&quot;/&gt;  on the Cumberland River, although in a better location, had a vulnerable land side and did not have enough heavy artillery to defend against gunboats.&lt;ref name=&quot;Woodworth56&quot;/&gt;

Maj. Gen. Polk ignored the problems of the forts when he took command in July 1861 because they were not in his jurisdiction. After Johnston took command and included the forts in Polk's area of authority, he at first refused to comply with Johnston's order to send an engineer, Lt. Joseph K. Dixon, to inspect the forts.&lt;ref name=&quot;Woodworth57&quot;&gt;Woodworth, p. 57.&lt;/ref&gt; After Johnston asserted his authority, Polk had to allow Dixon to proceed. Dixon recommended that the forts be maintained and strengthened, although they were not in ideal locations, because much work had been done on them, and the Confederates might not have time to build new ones. Johnston accepted his recommendations.&lt;ref name=&quot;Woodworth57&quot;/&gt; Johnston wanted Major  to command the forts, but President Davis appointed Brig. Gen.  as commander.&lt;ref name=&quot;Long142&quot;/&gt;&lt;ref name=&quot;Woodworth57&quot;/&gt; Alerted by a U.S. reconnaissance on January 14, 1862, Johnston ordered Tilghman to fortify the high ground opposite Fort Henry, which Polk had failed to do despite Johnston's orders.&lt;ref name=&quot;Woodworth71&quot;&gt;Woodworth, p. 71.&lt;/ref&gt; Tilghman failed to act decisively on these orders, which were too late to be adequately carried out in any event.&lt;ref name=&quot;Woodworth71&quot; /&gt;&lt;ref&gt;McPherson, p. 396.&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref&gt;A Confederate battery and the beginning of some fortifications were sited across the river at , but these were of little value when the U.S. flotilla appeared.&lt;/ref&gt; On January 20, 1862, Johnston ordered Floyd, Buckner, and 8,000 troops from Bowling Green to , Kentucky. Here they could respond to an advance from Buell's Army of the Ohio at , Kentucky, or to an offensive by Grant's forces at , Illinois, up the Cumberland River.

Gen. Beauregard arrived at Johnston's headquarters at Bowling Green on February 4, 1862, and was given overall command of Polk's force at the western end of Johnston's line at Columbus, Kentucky.&lt;ref&gt;Woodworth, p. 78.&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref&gt;After some preliminary work with Johnston, Beauregard assumed command of this force, which he named the Army of the Mississippi, on March 5, 1862, while at Jackson, Tennessee. Like the other Confederate commander, he had to withdraw to the south after the fall of the forts or be surrounded by the advancing U.S. forces. Long, p. 178.&lt;/ref&gt; Gen. Pillow was assigned to defend , Tennessee, with a small force. On February 6, 1862, U.S. gunboats attacked the ill-sited Fort Henry, which had flooded because of the unusually high rainfall in early 1862.&lt;ref name=&quot;Woodworth7879&quot;&gt;Woodworth, pp. 78–79.&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref name=&quot;Long167&quot;&gt;Long, p. 167.&lt;/ref&gt; Gen. Tilghman sent nearly all of his 3,000-man force to Fort Donelson, and remained at Fort Henry with 94 artillery men to fight it out with the gunboats. Several of the Confederate artillery pieces exploded or were destroyed during the combat and Tilghman was compelled to surrender Fort Henry.&lt;ref name=&quot;Woodworth7879&quot; /&gt;&lt;ref&gt;Long, pp. 166–167&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref&gt;Weigley, p. 109.&lt;/ref&gt; At a conference at Covington House in Bowling Green the next day, Johnston, Beauregard, and Hardee decided that the U.S. gunboats were invincible and that Fort Donelson was untenable. Johnston knew he could be trapped at Bowling Green if Fort Donelson fell, so he moved his force to , the capital of Tennessee and an increasingly important Confederate industrial center, beginning on February 11, 1862.&lt;ref name=&quot;Woodworth79&quot;&gt;Woodworth, p. 79.&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref&gt;Loing, pp. 169–170.&lt;/ref&gt;

After deciding that Fort Donelson was untenable on February 7, 1862, Johnston received intelligence from Buckner the next day reporting that Grant's army only numbered 12,000 men. In the next few days, Johnston received information from several officers describing the &quot;considerable damage suffered by the Union ironclads during the battle of Fort Henry.&quot;&lt;ref&gt;Goggin, pp. 217-218&lt;/ref&gt; These two pieces of information gave Johnston confidence that Fort Donelson could be defended. On February 12, 1862, Maj. Gen  informed a subordinate that &quot;General A.S. Johnston, from whom I heard yesterday, feels confident of holding Fort Donelson and driving the enemy from the Tennessee soon.&quot;&lt;ref&gt;Goggin, pp. 219&lt;/ref&gt; Johnston ordered Gen. Pillow and Gen. Floyd to concentrate their troops at Fort Donelson, confident that the 16,000 Confederate troops could defeat Grant's army and that Fort Donelson's batteries could repel the gunboats. Unfortunately for Johnston, the senior generals sent to the fort to command the enlarged garrison, Floyd, Pillow, and Buckner squandered their chance to achieve victory over Grant's forces when comparably sized, and became despondent when large Union reinforcements arrived on the night of February 13, 1862. After a failed breakout attempt on February 15, 1862, Gen. Buckner, having been abandoned by Floyd&lt;ref&gt;Floyd was able to ferry his four Virginia regiments out of the fort with him but left his Mississippi regiment behind to surrender with the rest of the garrison. Pillow escaped only with his chief of staff. Woodworth, p. 83. Long, p. 171.&lt;/ref&gt; and Pillow, surrendered Fort Donelson the next morning.&lt;ref&gt;Woodworth, pp. 82–84.&lt;/ref&gt; Colonel  escaped with his cavalry force of about 700 men before the surrender.&lt;ref&gt;Woodworth, p. 84.&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref&gt;McPherson, pp. 401–402.&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref&gt;This included about 200 men not in Forrest's immediate command. Weigley, p. 111&lt;/ref&gt; The Confederates suffered about 1,500 casualties, with an estimated 12,000 to 14,000 taken prisoner.&lt;ref&gt;Long, p. 172.&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref name=&quot;Weigley111&quot;&gt;Weigley, p. 111.&lt;/ref&gt; U.S. casualties were 500 killed, 2,108 wounded, and 224 missing.&lt;ref name=&quot;Weigley111&quot; /&gt;

Johnston, who had little choice in allowing Floyd and Pillow to take charge at Fort Donelson based on seniority after he ordered them to add their forces to the garrison, took the blame and suffered calls for his removal because a full explanation to the press and public would have exposed the weakness of the Confederate position.&lt;ref&gt;Woodworth, pp. 84–85.&lt;/ref&gt; His passive defensive performance while positioning himself in a forward position at Bowling Green, spreading his forces too thinly, not concentrating his forces in the face of U.S. advances, and appointing or relying upon inadequate or incompetent subordinates subjected him to criticism at the time and by later historians.&lt;ref&gt;Weigley, p. 112.&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref&gt;McPherson, pp. 405–406.&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref&gt;Davis defended Johnston, saying: &quot;If Sidney Johnston is not a general, we had better give up the war, for we have no general.&quot; McPherson, p. 495.&lt;/ref&gt; However, one Confederate officer observed that when Johnston assumed command in September 1861, he had &quot;found an army of hastily levied volunteers, badly equipped, miserably clad, fully one half stricken down by disease, destitute of transportation, and with barely the shadow of discipline... with these men he held at bay a force of the enemy of fully 100,000 men... The Southern States were protected from invasion. Time was obtained to drill and consolidate the volunteer force. The army was sustained in the fertile and abundant grain-producing regions of Kentucky, transportation gathered of the most efficient character, immense supplies of beef, corn, and pork collected from the surrounding country and safely garnered in depots further South for the coming summer campaign.&quot;&lt;ref&gt;Goggin, pp. 247-248&lt;/ref&gt; Johnston had held his position for six months but the fall of the forts exposed Nashville to an imminent attack, and it fell without resistance to U.S. forces under Gen. Buell on February 25, 1862, two days after Johnston had to pull his forces out to avoid having them captured as well.&lt;ref name=&quot;Woodworth86&quot;&gt;Woodworth, p. 86.&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref&gt;Long, p. 175.&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref&gt;McPherson, p. 402.&lt;/ref&gt;


Johnston was in a perilous situation after the fall of Ft. Donelson and Henry; with barely 17,000 men to face an overwhelming concentration of Union force, he hastily fled south into Mississippi by way of Nashville and then into northern Alabama.&lt;ref&gt;Woodworth, pp. 85–86.&lt;/ref&gt; Johnston himself retreated with the force under his personal command, the , from the vicinity of Nashville.&lt;ref name=&quot;Woodworth86&quot;/&gt; With Beauregard's help,&lt;ref name=&quot;McPherson, p. 406&quot;&gt;McPherson, p. 406.&lt;/ref&gt; Johnston decided to concentrate forces with those formerly under Polk and now already under Beauregard's command at the strategically located railroad crossroads of , which he reached by a circuitous route.&lt;ref&gt;Woodworth, pp. 86–88.&lt;/ref&gt; Johnston kept the U.S. forces, now under the overall command of Maj. Gen. , confused and hesitant to move, allowing Johnston to reach his objective undetected.&lt;ref&gt;Woodworth, p. 88.&lt;/ref&gt; He scraped together reinforcements from Louisiana, as well as part of Polk's force at Island No. 10, and 10,000 additional troops under Gen. Bragg brought up from Mobile.&lt;ref&gt;Woodworth, pp. 90, 94.&lt;/ref&gt; Bragg at least calmed the nerves of Beauregard and Polk, who had become agitated by their apparent dire situation in the face of numerically superior forces, before Johnston's arrival on March 24, 1862.&lt;ref name=&quot;Woodworth95&quot;&gt;Woodworth, p. 95.&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref&gt;Long, p. 188.&lt;/ref&gt;

Johnston's army of 17,000 men gave the Confederates a combined force of about 40,000 to 44,669 men at Corinth.&lt;ref name=&quot;Woodworth95&quot;/&gt;&lt;ref name=&quot;McPherson, p. 406&quot;/&gt;&lt;ref&gt;Eicher, ''The Longest Night'', p. 223.&lt;/ref&gt; On March 29, 1862, Johnston officially took command of this combined force, which continued to use the Army of the Mississippi name under which Beauregard had organized it on March 5.&lt;ref&gt;Long, 190.&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref&gt;Eicher, ''Civil War High Commands'' p. 887 and Eicher, ''The Longest Night'' p. 219 are nearly alone in referring to this army as the Army of Mississippi. Muir, p. 85, in discussing the first &quot;Army of Mississippi&quot;, includes this army as one of three in the article with that title but states: &quot;Historians have pointed out that the Army of Mississippi is frequently mentioned in the Official Records as the Army of the Mississippi.&quot; Contemporaries, including Johnston and Beauregard, and modern historians call this Confederate army the Army of the Mississippi. , Volume X, Part 1, index, pp. 96–99; 385 (Beauregard's report on the Battle of Shiloh, April 11, 1862, from Headquarters, Army of the Mississippi) and Part 2, p. 297 (Beauregard's announcement on taking command of Army of the Mississippi); p. 370 (Johnston General Orders of March 29, 1862, assuming command and announcing the army would retain the name Army of the Mississippi); pp. 405–409. Beauregard, p. 579. Boritt, p. 53. Connelly, ''Army of the Heartland: The Army of Tennessee, 1861–1862''. p. 151. (&quot;The Army retained Beauregard's chosen name...&quot;) Connelly, ''Civil War Tennessee: Battles And Leaders''. p. 35. Cunningham, pp. 98, 122, 397. Engle, p. 123. Hattaway, p. 163. Hess, pp. 47, 49, 112 (&quot;...Braxton Bragg's renamed Army of Tennessee (formerly the Army of the Mississippi)...&quot;). Isbell, p. 102. McDonough, pp. 60, 66, 78. Kennedy, p. 48. Noe, p. 19. Williams, p. 122.&lt;/ref&gt;

Johnston's only hope was to crush Grant before Buell and others could reinforce him.&lt;ref name=&quot;Woodworth95&quot;/&gt; He started his army in motion on April 3, intent on surprising Grant's force as soon as the next day. It was not an easy undertaking; his army had been hastily thrown together, two-thirds of the soldiers had never fired a shot in battle, and drill, discipline, and staff work were so poor that the different divisions kept stumbling into each other on the march.&lt;ref&gt;Woodworth, pp. 96–97.&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref&gt;Long, p. 192&lt;/ref&gt; Beauregard felt that this offensive was a mistake and could not possibly succeed, but Johnston replied &quot;I would fight them if they were a million&quot; as he drove his army on to Pittsburg Landing.&lt;ref&gt;McWhiney; Jamieson, p. 162.&lt;/ref&gt; His army was finally in position within a mile or two of Grant's force, undetected, by the evening of April 5, 1862.&lt;ref&gt;Woodworth, p. 97.&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref&gt;Long, pp. 193–194.&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref&gt;Weigley, p. 113.&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref&gt;McPherson, pp. 406–407.&lt;/ref&gt;&lt;ref&gt;Johnston did not achieve total surprise as some U.S. pickets were alerted to the Confederate presence and provided warning to some U.S. units before the attack began.&lt;/ref&gt;


Johnston launched a massive surprise attack with his concentrated forces against Grant at the  on April 6, 1862.&lt;ref&gt;Chisholm, p. 473&lt;/ref&gt; As the Confederate forces overran the U.S. camps, Johnston personally rallied troops up and down the line on his horse. One of his famous moments in the battle occurred when he witnessed some of his soldiers breaking from the ranks to pillage and loot the U.S. camps and was outraged to see a young lieutenant among them. &quot;None of that, sir&quot;, Johnston roared at the officer, &quot;we are not here for plunder.&quot; Then, realizing he had embarrassed the man, he picked up a tin cup from a table and announced, &quot;Let this be my share of the spoils today&quot;, before directing his army onward.&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt;

At about 2:30 pm, while leading one of those charges against a U.S. camp near the &quot;Peach Orchard&quot;, he was wounded, taking a bullet behind his right knee. The bullet clipped a part of his , and his boot filled up with blood. No medical personnel were on the scene since Johnston had sent his personal surgeon to care for the wounded Confederate troops and U.S. prisoners earlier in the battle.&lt;ref name=&quot;civilwarlandscapes.org&quot;&gt;&lt;/ref&gt;'s drawing of the death of General Johnston]]

Within a few minutes, Johnston was observed by his staff to be nearly fainting. Among his staff was , the , who had ceased to make any real effort to function as governor after learning that  had appointed  as military governor of Tennessee. Seeing Johnston slumping in his saddle and his face turning deathly pale, Harris asked: &quot;General, are you wounded?&quot; Johnston said his last words in a weak voice: &quot;Yes... and I fear seriously.&quot; Harris and other staff officers removed Johnston from his horse, carried him to a small ravine near the &quot;Hornets Nest&quot;, and desperately tried to aid the general, who had lost consciousness. They could not find the fatal wound and Harris sent an aide to fetch Johnston's surgeon. A few minutes later, Johnston died from blood loss before a doctor could be found. An examination of the case by modern neurosurgeons reported that &quot;based on the description of the completely severed popliteal artery... General Johnston, sitting in the saddle of his horse with his leg extended, would quickly lose consciousness and bleed to death within a few minutes of the injury described by his surgeon.&quot; Harris believed that if the tourniquet found in Johnston's pocket had been applied the general could have been saved, but the neurosurgeons stated that &quot;in actual battlefield medical practice, by the time they navigated Johnston on his horse with his leg extended (and bleeding) to a safe place, the blood loss may have already led to his death, even if the wound was immediately identified.&quot;&lt;ref&gt;Goggin, pp. 362&lt;/ref&gt;]]Harris and the other officers wrapped General Johnston's body in a blanket to not damage the troops' morale with the sight of the dead general. Johnston and his wounded horse, Fire Eater, were taken to his field headquarters on the Corinth road, where his body remained in his tent for the remainder of the battle. P. G. T. Beauregard assumed command of the army. He resumed leading the Confederate assault, which continued advancing and pushed the U.S. forces back to a final defensive line near the Tennessee river. With his army exhausted and daylight almost gone, Beauregard called off the final Confederate attack around 1900 hours, figuring he could finish off the U.S. army the following morning. However, Grant was reinforced by 20,000 fresh troops from Gen. Buell's Army of the Ohio during the night and led a successful counter-attack the following day, driving the Confederates from the field and winning the battle. As the Confederate army retreated to Corinth, Johnston's body was taken to the home of Colonel William Inge, which had been his headquarters in Corinth. It was covered in the Confederate flag and lay in state for several hours.&lt;ref&gt;Sword, pp. 270–273, 443–446; Cunningham, pp. 273–276; Smith, pp. 26–34. Sword offers evidence that Johnston lived as long as an hour after receiving his fatal wound.&lt;/ref&gt;

It is possible that a Confederate soldier fired the fatal round, as many Confederates were firing at the U.S. lines while Johnston charged well in advance of his soldiers.&lt;ref&gt;Sword, p. 444.&lt;/ref&gt; However, historian Timothy B. Smith noted: &quot;A bullet had entered the back of the leg. This sparked some wild speculation that the general was shot from the rear by one of his own men, despite the fact that a horseman could at any time be facing any direction on a spirited and excited mount that was also in the process of being wounded multiple times.&quot;  of Los Angeles commanded the bodyguard &quot;the Guides&quot; of Gen. A. S. Johnston and was by his side when he fell.&lt;ref&gt; ''Los Angeles Star,'' Vol. XII, No. 30, November 29, 1862.&lt;/ref&gt; Johnston was the highest-ranking fatality of the war on either side and his death was a strong blow to the morale of the Confederacy. At the time, Davis considered him the best general in the country.&lt;ref&gt;Dupuy, p. 378.&lt;/ref&gt;



In 1829, Johnston married Henrietta Preston, sister of Kentucky politician and future Civil War general . They had three children at Jefferson Barracks, of whom two survived to adulthood. Their son, , became a colonel in the Confederate States Army.&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt; Their daughter, also named Henrietta Preston, never married. In 1834, the senior Johnston resigned his commission to care for his dying wife in Kentucky, who succumbed two years later to .&lt;ref name=Woodworth46/&gt; In 1843, Johnston married , his late wife's first cousin. The couple had a son, Albert Sidney Jr., when living in Shelbyville, Kentucky. They had two more children at the China Grove plantation in Texas, of whom one, Hancock McClung, survived to adulthood. A daughter, Margaret Strother, was born in Austin in 1851, followed by a third son, Griffin, in 1857. A sixth child, Eliza Alberta, was born when the family lived in Los Angeles, where they had permanently settled.&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt;


 by  in the  in ]]

Johnston was survived by his wife, Eliza, and six children. His wife and five younger children, including one born after he went to war, chose to live out their days at home in Los Angeles with Eliza's brother, Dr. .&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt; Johnston's eldest son, Albert Sidney Jr. (born in Texas), had already followed him into the Confederate States Army. In 1863, Albert Jr. was on his way out of  harbor on a ferry after taking home leave in Los Angeles. While a  was taking on passengers from the ferry, a wave swamped the smaller boat, causing its boilers to explode. Albert Jr. was killed in the accident.&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt;

Upon his passing, General Johnston received the highest praise ever given by the Confederate government: accounts were published on December 20, 1862, and after that, in the Los Angeles ''Star'' of his family's hometown.&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt; Johnston Street, Hancock Street, and Griffin Avenue, each in , are named after the general and his family, who lived in the neighborhood.

Johnston was initially buried in . In 1866, a joint resolution of the  was passed to have his body moved and reinterred at the  in . The re-interment occurred in 1867.&lt;ref name=&quot;Monthly&quot;&gt;&lt;/ref&gt; Forty years later, the state appointed  to design  of him to be erected at the grave site, installed in 1905.&lt;ref name=&quot;TSC&quot;&gt;&lt;/ref&gt;

The  has erected a historical marker near the entrance of what was once Johnston's . An adjacent marker was erected by the San Jacinto Chapter of the  and the Lee, Roberts, and Davis Chapter of the .

In 1916, the University of Texas at Austin recognized several confederate veterans (including Johnston) with statues on its South Mall. On August 21, 2017, as part of the wave of ,  was taken down. Plans were announced to add it to the  on the east side of the university campus.&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt;

Johnston was inducted to the  in 1980.&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt;

In the fall of 2018, A. S. Johnston Elementary School in Dallas, Texas, was renamed Cedar Crest Elementary. Johnston Middle School in Houston, Texas, was also renamed Meyerland Middle School. Three other elementary schools named for Confederate veterans were renamed simultaneously.&lt;ref&gt;&lt;/ref&gt;
